extracted.intended_audience: naval architects, ship designers, marine engineers, and maritime regulators
extracted.subtask_description: A critical review of unresolved problems and evaluation criteria in ship design and propulsion, covering safety (loading, freeboard, bulkheads, stability), structural strength, resistance and model testing, propeller efficiency, and requirements for marine engines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum depth of safe loading / minimum sea-going freeboard
rubrics_metrics.description: The first in natural order of the problems that relate to safety is the maximum depth of safe loading, or the minimum sea-going freeboard for a ship of any given size or type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeboard rules and tables should embody results of safe loading and prevent dangerous overloading. Historical example: Board of Trade freeboard rules arrived at by committee (first official tables prepared 1885). Designers and authorities should use analysed experience to frame rules/tables of freeboard. Enforcement and association with protection of openings greatly reduce losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of openings on the weather-deck
rubrics_metrics.description: Close attention to the protection of openings in the weather-deck is an important element of safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection of deck openings, together with freeboard regulation, has resulted in an extraordinary diminution of losses at sea; these measures should be integral to safety regulations and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of hull into separate watertight compartments (bulkheads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hull subdivision into separate water-tight compartments to guard against foundering after collision is an important element of safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions and number of watertight bulkheads are often regulated to carry out recommendations (e.g., Board of Trade Bulkheads Committee, 1891). Compliance with such committee rules is optional for shipowners, and full compliance is not general; designers should consider these recommendations when fixing bulkhead positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability (metacentric height) and its dependence on loading/stowage
rubrics_metrics.description: The stability of a ship when floating in equilibrium (represented by righting-moment curves and metacentric height) is readily calculated for still-water conditions but can vary significantly under service conditions depending on loading and stowage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must judge what metacentric height to provide by comparison with ships of similar successful types. Official bodies assigning load-lines should seek proof that dangers from homogeneous cargo stowage (which can dangerously reduce stability) are understood and will be guarded against. Examples given of metacentric-height variation due to water-ballast use and service loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stowage practices as a determinant of ship safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper stowage is essential to secure stability and therefore ship safety; stability cannot be ensured by design alone if stowage is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vessels could be loaded with homogeneous cargoes that reduce stability, authorities should require proof that stowage will be regulated to prevent danger. Designers and regulators must account for operator-controlled stowage practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural strength (especially longitudinal strength) and limits of calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural strength is a central and intricate problem; usual calculations of strength (often based on still-water conditions) do not by themselves carry us very far in shipbuilding, particularly for longitudinal stresses which are the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of structure has largely followed experience and classification societies (Lloyd's) rules. Calculations often rest on assumptions that differ from real circumstances and may be in excess of the truth; designers must use judgment, observation, and empirical evidence, and treat calculated quantitative stresses cautiously. Wave-support hypotheses (e.g., ship supported on wave-crest/hollows) are used to approximate worst conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of actual stresses at sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to measure real stresses on ship structure at sea (using strain indicators) have been made but have yielded limited quantitative progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments (e.g., Admiralty Committee using Stromeyer's indicators on H.M.S. Colla) gave interesting results; more and better in-service measurements are needed to approach a quantitative solution to the strength problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with classification society rules as a structural design guide
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of material and sizes of structural parts are often determined by compliance with Lloyd's Register Society rules and tables, which are modified as ships change in size and type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is important for insurance; when ships are exceptional, Lloyd's deals specially with structural design. The governing principle is experience of ship behaviour at sea, supplemented by Lloyd's technical research staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for requisite strength with minimum material weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain the requisite structural strength with the minimum weight of material — a very difficult problem scientifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons (e.g., Great Eastern vs modern ships) indicate possibilities for novel structural arrangements that could save weight and cost and help with draught restrictions. Careful investigation is warranted before radically changing structural design of large ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed problem: use of model experiments and Froude's law of similitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of a ship's resistance and hence power required for a given speed is practically solved by Froude's law of similitude, enabling resistance of models to be used to predict full-scale ship resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers need the means to ascertain resistance at desired speeds and to determine hull form (degree of fineness) giving maximum carrying power at moderate fuel consumption. Froude's systematic model experiments provide resistance data for families of typical lines and block coefficients; similar datasets for other ship types would be valuable. Where a national experimental tank is unavailable, designers face limitations and may need to go abroad or use published systematic data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for accessible national experimental tank and expert staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate model testing requires not only a tank and apparatus but a competent, experienced staff; results depend heavily on experimenters' personal qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental tanks are costly and require high-quality personnel; the absence of a national public tank for general use limits designers. The National Physical Laboratory attempt was without result; private and Admiralty tanks exist but are often restricted to owners' use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screw-propeller efficiency and scale limitations of model tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of engine power from resistance requires knowledge of screw-propeller efficiency, but model experiments so far have used very small screws limited by apparatus stresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further advance may come from larger-scale experiments with stronger appliances or an experimental launch run in open water (as proposed by R. E. Froude) that could allow experimentation with much larger screw diameters (up to ~3 ft) and automatically record thrust and torque — bringing propeller efficiency closer to practical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off of hull form (block coefficient) for carrying power vs fuel consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: For any particular trade or service, determine the hull form and degree of fullness (block coefficient) that gives maximum passenger and freight-carrying capacity with moderate engine power and fuel expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic model data across ranges of block coefficients (e.g., 0.4865 to 0.541 for certain Channel-boat types) let designers select proportions and forms. Extending such data to fast-liner types (block coefficients ~0.6–0.7) would aid designers of those vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and assessment of propelling machinery (turbine vs reciprocating vs internal-combustion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether marine turbines, reciprocating engines, or internal-combustion engines best meet the needs of the vessel class, with main criterion being fuel consumption/economy and proven reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of turbines depends largely on whether fuel consumption can match best reciprocating engines; Cunard's experiments with turbines in liners are pivotal. Warship and cross-Channel reciprocating-engine consumption (about 17 lb/I.H.P.-hr) vs ocean-liner quadruple-expansion figures (~13 lb/I.H.P.-hr) set benchmarks. The choice also depends on measurement of turbine power and long-run practical experience. High stakes in large liners make operators cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate measurement of turbine power (torque and output)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct measurement of power given out by turbine machinery is a practical problem of great importance; methods like telephonic recording of shaft twist have been used but are not always sufficiently accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory solution for recording torque and hence power is much required for designers to assess turbine performance and fuel economy reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required of a successful marine engine (enumerated requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful marine engine of any type must satisfy a list of operational and safety conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated conditions (as listed): (1) The engine must be reversible; (2) capable of being stopped quickly, and of being started quickly either ahead or astern; (3) capable of being promptly speeded to any desired revolutions between dead slow and full speed and kept steadily at required speed for any length of time ('dead slow' about one-quarter of full speed or less in very fast vessels); (4) capable of running continuously for long distances with short intervals between runs without risk of stoppage or breakdown; (5) work well in heavy weather and varying immersion of the propeller; (6) all working parts readily accessible for overhauling and wearing surfaces promptly and easily adjustable; (7) economical in fuel, especially at ordinary working speed; (8) compact, light in weight, and well balanced so as not to cause vibration; (9) must not involve risk of accumulation of gas in the ship which could form an explosive mixture.
